Earth Looks Like It's Dripping. Your Map Never Said Why
The Continents Are Pointing at Something
A 400-Year-Old Clue in the Shape of the Continents
Why Every Map Looks Like It's Dripping South
Why Earth Drips South, and Where It's Dripping Next
thumbnail_concepts: CAN'T UNSEE IT (UNSEE in pure red #FF2B2B, not the #FF5A36 land hue; white text on black boxes, top-left). Built from the EXACT frame-1 render (s001: same ~60 deg underside tilt and crop) so 0:00 matches. South America and Africa tapers fill the lower-middle third, large and glowing orange; India secondary. Three thick white drip-arrows from Cape Froward, Cape Agulhas and Kanyakumari run into a yellow #FFD23F ring at bottom centre with a white '?' inside (the unresolved question). Atmosphere and night lights off for 120-px legibility. Pair with title 1 or 3.

POINTING AT WHAT? (WHAT in red). Same frame-1 render; the three drip-arrows stop at the edge of the yellow ring and the white '?' inside it is enlarged. The title says 'south'; the thumbnail opens the deeper gap the video pays off at s074 and s079-s081 (they point back to Antarctica). Pair with title 1 or 3.

THEY POINT HERE (HERE in red; deliberately not 'ALL'). Same frame-1 render plus dotted ghost outlines of South America, Africa and India snapped into the yellow ring (the s007 one-second flash frame) and one fat white arrow aimed at the ring. No Australia slab (Australia's Cape York points north, s091). Shows the shape of the answer without explaining it. Pair with title 1. Test all three with Test & Compare on title 1, judged on watch-time share; check at 120 px next to RealLifeLore / Johnny Harris. Optional 4th (story) arm, only with title 4: same globe, torn sepia strip top-right, '"NOT AN ACCIDENT"' in quote marks with a small 1620 tag (matches the s106 ending line).

chapters.title: Why does Earth look like it's dripping?
Why did geologists laugh at Wegener?
Where is the drip going next?

segments.text: Spin a globe, and Earth looks like it's {m:melt}melting.
segments.visual: FRAME 1 = THUMBNAIL IN MOTION (same render as thumbnail T1). globeShot keys {lat:-30, lon:20, alt:3.0, tilt:0, heading:0}, drift 2 deg/s; look {desat:0.3, dim:0.35, ovAlpha:1}; ocean navy #0A1A2E. One fillEquirect overlay: South America, Africa, India in #FF5A36, glow 24. A #FFD23F ring with a white '?' inside pulses on the South Pole (1.2 s period). At {m:melt}: three `arcs` draw on (1.0 s each, staggered 0.15 s, white, lift 0.08, headDot) from Cape Froward (-53.9,-71.3), Cape Agulhas (-34.8,20.0) and Kanyakumari (8.1,77.5) to (-78,20); then the three glows fade back to 30% over 0.3 s so s002 can re-light them.
segments.music: Cold open: pulsing low synth bed, tense and minimal, starts on frame 1.

segments.text: {m:sam}South America. {m:afr}Africa. {m:ind}India.
segments.visual: No camera travel (s001 view holds). On each marker the named landmass snaps back to full orange and a white outline of its southern tip draws on (strokeProjected, 0.35 s): {m:sam} Cape Froward, {m:afr} Cape Agulhas (NOT the Cape of Good Hope), {m:ind} Kanyakumari. No labels needed.

segments.text: {m:grl}Greenland. {m:fla}Florida. {m:baja}Baja. {m:kam}Kamchatka.
segments.visual: Hard cut on {m:grl} (6-frame whoosh) to the EQUAL EARTH FLAT MAP (new mode: one precomputed still, inverse-projected from tex/day_8k.jpg, 30% desat, navy ocean, faint graticule; markers placed with the forward Equal Earth formula). South America, Africa and India are already orange. Each tip fills orange with a white outline on its word: Cape Farewell 59.8N 43.9W; Cape Sable 25.3N 81.1W and Cabo San Lucas 22.9N 109.9W (tips_admin1); Cape Lopatka 50.9N 156.7E (tips_admin1 Kamchatka). One pill at a time, each fading as the next pops. TTS: check 'Baja' (BAH-hah) and 'Kamchatka' (kam-CHAHT-kuh) before lock; alias in TTS input only.

segments.text: Every point aims {m:south}south. Like somebody left the planet on the dashboard in {m:july}July.
segments.visual: Flat map holds. At {m:south}: all seven tips get a short #FFD23F drip arrow pointing straight down (len 70 px, staggered 0.06 s). At {m:july}: hard cut to EXPLORER GAG 1 (~3 s, separate stage): tinyPlanet radius 3, rotated so Cape Agulhas sits just in front of the top point, warm 2D sun flare top-right. An orange 3D teardrop (sphere + cone, 0.25 units) swells at the cape and slides down the planet's front curve. The Explorer walks to the edge (Walk 0.4 s), reaches down to catch it (Interact 1.0 s); the drop slips past his fingers and falls off into space; he wobbles at the edge (HitRecieve_2). Cut on the wobble into s005.
segments.humor: Narration: the planet left on the dashboard in July (melting-crayon image). EXPLORER GAG 1: tries to catch the drip and nearly falls off Africa (Walk, Interact, HitRecieve_2).
sfx: cartoon_fall (-10) on the wobble (the only fall whistle in the video)

segments.text: {m:twothirds}Two-thirds of all land is north of the {m:eq}equator. So are nearly {m:nine}nine in ten of us.
segments.visual: Photoreal globe {lat:15, lon:20, alt:3.2}. At {m:twothirds}: setOverlayURL('tex/data/land_north.png') fades in orange while look.dim rises to 0.45 (southern land darkens). At {m:eq}: a glowing white equator ring draws on (1.0 s) and a two-part split bar (right third, above the bottom 12%) fills to the two-thirds mark, no digits. At {m:nine}: land overlay drops to 30%; white dots for every city in ne_110m_populated_places_simple pop in (radius proportional to sqrt(pop_max)), heavily northern; the bar refills to the nine-in-ten mark.

segments.text: You've probably heard those southern points are just a {m:coin}coincidence.
segments.visual: Globe keeps drifting. At {m:coin}: a 2D gold coin spins up in front of the globe (scaleX oscillation, 1.5 turns/s). Generic coin only: no channel names, no thumbnails of other videos.

segments.text: They're {m:not}not. Not {m:entirely}entirely.
segments.visual: Music cut 0.5 s before 'They're'. At {m:not}: the coin freezes and cracks in two. At {m:entirely}: a 1.0 s UNEXPLAINED flash of the final answer: paleo globe from a south-polar camera (paleo/coast_180.json) with South America, Africa and India clamped around Antarctica's yellow ring, then snap back to today's tilted globe.
segments.music: Bed returns heavier after the cut.

segments.text: So {m:why}why do the continents point south? By the end, you'll know what they're really {m:pointing}pointing at.
segments.visual: Slow push-in on the s001 tilted globe; the three drip arcs redraw and converge on Antarctica's ring with the white '?'. Kinetic headline (F.headline) lands on the question. At {m:pointing} the ring flares. SHORTS CUT ends here; for the Short replace the second sentence with 'The full story is on the channel.' MARKER CUES: {m:why} the kinetic headline starts rising word by word.
onscreen: WHY DO THE CONTINENTS POINT SOUTH?

segments.text: Along the way: why you can't dig to China from {m:usa}anywhere in America.
segments.visual: Teaser, nothing explained. At {m:usa}: 1.8 s hard cut to the cutawayEarth stage, shell rotated so Kansas is on top (setFromUnitVectors(llDir(39.83,-98.58), up)); drillDir grows the cyan line from the top through the core and out the bottom in 1.2 s; a yellow '?' pops at the exit. Camera st.lookFrom([6,3.5,6],[0,0.3,0],32).

segments.text: A theory from {m:t1875}eighteen seventy-five that explained all of it, and was {m:wrong}dead wrong. And {m:last}the last one: the four continents your country might {m:crash}crash into. Eventually.
segments.visual: At {m:t1875}: 0.8 s sepia flash of Green's Figure 5 (assets/pd/green_fig45.jpg, lower half), then the tetraEarth stage with k 0->1 over 1.5 s (yellow edges). At {m:wrong}: it snaps back to a sphere (k 1->0, E.outBack) under a red X stamp. At {m:last}: cut to the cold-open globe spinning forward fast. At {m:crash}: 1.0 s flash of the 2x2 grid of the four model end-state stills (pre-rendered in s099-s102), the white US marker pulsing in every tile; no single neighbor is shown. Hard cut to black on 'Eventually'.
segments.humor: 'Eventually.' undercuts the doom.
sfx: impact_deep (-6) on the cut to black

segments.text: Bad news: you're not the first to notice. {m:bacon}Not even close.
segments.visual: From black, fade up on the s003 Equal Earth flat map with the seven orange tips. A sepia paper wash wipes left to right across it (sepia grade, grain 10) while a year counter top-left (JetBrains Mono) rolls back 2026 -> 1620. At {m:bacon}: cross-dissolve to the 1620 Instauratio Magna engraved title page (assets/pd/title_1620.jpg) in a rounded print frame; Ken Burns from the galleon (cx 0.5, cy 0.75, zoom 1.6) up to the title (0.5, 0.3, 1.15).
segments.humor: Self-aware 'bad news' for the viewer.
segments.music: Switch to felt piano + soft strings for the history.

segments.text: In sixteen twenty, Francis {m:fb}Bacon wrote that the Old World and the New are both {m:narrow}'narrow and pointed toward the south.'
segments.visual: At {m:fb}: Ken Burns on Bacon's portrait (assets/pd/bacon.jpg, Paul van Somer 1617, sepia print frame). At {m:narrow}: cut to the 1620 page that actually holds the passage: archive.org instauratiomagna00baco leaf n246 = printed p.239 (research/script/visual-director/dl_ia/n246.jpg; NOT assets/pd/bacon_p232.jpg, which is p.240 and lacks it). Ken Burns into lines 4-6; an orange glowPath underline draws under 'acuminati' (normalized box x0.568 y0.229 w0.130 h0.022) and the pill swaps to the Latin gloss. Then the Parasceve page (leaf n387 = printed p.20, dl_ia/n387.jpg) slides in from the right with an underline under 'ad Austrum angusta & veluti acuminata' (x0.154 y0.334 w0.517 h0.019) and a small 'x2' stamp: he wrote it twice. Visual only, no narration.

segments.text: And in the same {m:breath}breath, he said Africa and South America's matching capes were {m:accident}'not to be attributed to mere accident.'
segments.visual: 0-2.3 s: globe {lat:-25, lon:-10, alt:2.6}, Africa and South America outlined white side by side, their southern capes pulsing orange. At {m:breath}: back to page n246 and tilt the Ken Burns UP two lines from 'acuminati' (it is literally the sentence above, on the same 1620 page). At {m:accident}: orange underlines draw under 'quod non temere ac-' (x0.553 y0.131 w0.276 h0.017) and 'cidit.' (x0.079 y0.153 w0.064 h0.016); the English pill fades in. This proves thumbnail/title wording by ~1:05.
onscreen: "NOT TO BE ATTRIBUTED TO MERE ACCIDENT"
segments.music: Soft piano accent on 'accident'.

segments.text: Then he wrote down an open question: is there even a {m:southcont}southern continent down there? Nobody would lay eyes on {m:antar}Antarctica for two more {m:cent}centuries. Remember {m:rem}that.
segments.visual: Camera dives to the bottom of the globe at {m:southcont}; Antarctica is hidden under a soft white fog (white Antarctica polygon in the overlay canvas, feathered) with a hand-lettered '?'. A sepia year ticker flicks 1620 -> 1820 and the fog thins; freeze-drift on the '?' (drift keeps it alive). MARKER CUES: {m:antar} the sepia ticker starts 1620 -> 1820; {m:cent} the fog thins; {m:rem} hold-drift on the '?'.

segments.text: Now, you may have heard that Bacon predicted continental drift. {m:scratch}He didn't.
segments.visual: Globe {lat:-15, lon:-15, alt:2.4}: South America's rings drag (moves, true size) toward Africa and rotate to snap into its coast. At {m:scratch}: frozen mid-snap, a red JUICE CHECK: FALSE stamp slams down (brand verdict device, first use).
segments.humor: Record-scratch myth-bust.

segments.text: He wasn't {m:snap}snapping Africa and South America together like puzzle pieces. He was saying they're shaped {m:same}alike, side by side.
segments.visual: The jigsaw rewinds (South America slides back home). At {m:same}: both continents sit side by side in today's orientation; a white isosceles taper triangle draws over each, same orientation, with an approx-equals sign between them. MARKER CUES: {m:snap} the jigsaw rewind starts.

segments.text: So Bacon saw the drip, but never tried to {m:explain}explain it. For centuries, nobody else {m:anyone}could. That did not stop them from {m:try}trying.
segments.visual: Page n246 shrinks into a print frame top-left over the slowly turning drip globe. At {m:explain}: a big '?' draws on Antarctica's ring. At {m:anyone}: archival pages drop onto a stack, one every 1.1 s: Forster 1778 p.13 (fetch archive.org b30408623 page 13), Green 1875 preface (vestigesmolteng00greegoog leaf n7), Guyot 1849 p.22 (fetch earthmanlectures00guyo page 22). At {m:try}: the pile overflows the frame and topples off sideways.
segments.humor: Dry understatement: 'That did not stop them from trying.'

segments.text: Captain {m:cook}Cook's naturalist, Johann Reinhold Forster, claimed that every great southern tip looks {m:alike}alike: high, rocky, the end of a {m:mtn}mountain chain.
segments.visual: 0-2.6 s: Ken Burns on assets/pd/forster.png (Bause after Graff) in a sepia print frame. At {m:alike}: cut to the globe, relief 1.0, patch tex/patch/s_america_tip.jpg, camera low over Cape Froward looking north up the Andes {lat:-52, lon:-72, alt:0.25, tilt:55, heading:0}. At {m:mtn}: whip to Kanyakumari (patch s_india.jpg, tilt 55) looking north up the Western Ghats. Show only real terrain; draw NO 'mountain chain' lines from Cape Agulhas or Tasmania (Forster's rule is his claim, not ours). MARKER CUES: {m:cook} the Forster portrait Ken Burns starts.

segments.text: His {m:expl}explanation? A giant flood came {m:wave}roaring in from the south-west and {m:carved}carved every one of them. Some of the top scientists of the day {m:bought}bought it. Geology later asked for a {m:refund}refund.
segments.visual: On 'His explanation?': the fetched Forster 1778 p.13 scan, orange underline under 'a violent flood coming from the south-west'. At {m:wave}: cut to EXPLORER GAG 2 and stay there: tiny planet with the South Atlantic facing camera; a flat stylised 2D wave (cyan crest, white foam line) sweeps from lower-left (south-west) to upper-right over 1.4 s. The Explorer runs (Run_Right) but too late; the crest clips him (HitRecieve); it passes, and he stands soaked (Idle_Neutral) while a drop falls off his beard (now he's the one dripping). At {m:bought}: a small sepia wax seal stamps onto the wave graphic. At {m:refund}: the wave deflates like a pool float (scaleY 1 -> 0.1, 0.4 s). MARKER CUES: {m:expl} the Forster p.13 underline draws; {m:carved} the crest clips the Explorer (HitRecieve).
segments.humor: EXPLORER GAG 2: soaked by Forster's imaginary flood (Run_Right, HitRecieve, Idle_Neutral). Tag: 'Geology later asked for a refund.'

segments.text: By the eighteen-forties, the most famous scientist alive was calling the tips {m:pyr}'pyramidal.' And someone had written down almost the exact {m:list}list you saw at the start.
segments.visual: 2.5 s Ken Burns on Humboldt's portrait (Stieler 1843, PD; fetch from Commons) in a sepia frame. At {m:pyr}: cut to the s001 tilted globe; thin white triangle outlines snap onto the southern ends of South America, Africa and India (plants the pyramid for Chapter 3). At {m:list}: Ken Burns on the fetched Guyot 1849 p.22 scan.

segments.text: {m:l1}Greenland, {m:l2}Baja, {m:l3}Florida, {m:l4}India, {m:l5}Kamchatka. 'All their points turned towards the south.'
segments.visual: Match-cut to the EXACT s003 Equal Earth framing; re-pop the five tips in the same rhythm and with the same pop_ui thump as 0:04 (callback). The quote types on last.
onscreen: "ALL THEIR POINTS TURNED TOWARDS THE SOUTH"
sfx: pop_ui (-14) x5, same as the cold open

segments.text: Then, in the {m:seventies}nineteen-seventies, the pattern got its name, as a {m:joke}joke. A magazine writer called it {m:drip}'continental drip': a fake theory you could prove just by {m:staring}staring at a map.
segments.visual: Typewriter card on cream paper (JetBrains Mono 500; generic, no real magazine branding). At {m:joke}: a coffee-stained sheet slides in. At {m:drip}: 'CONTINENTAL DRIFT' types out, then the 'FT' is struck through and a 'P' typed over it: DRIP. MARKER CUES: {m:seventies} the '1973' pill pops; {m:staring} a magnifying-glass icon sweeps across a small world-map card.
segments.humor: DRIFT gets retyped as DRIP on screen.
segments.music: Light, playful pizzicato under the joke.

segments.text: Three years later, a geologist published his own {m:version}version of the joke. Hold on to {m:hold}him. He matters more than you'd {m:think}think.
segments.visual: A second typewriter sheet slides in behind the first; its byline is blurred. At {m:hold}: a yellow ring circles the blur; slow push-in. On 'more than you'd think': a 0.5 s flicker of the Gondwana paleo still behind the paper, like a watermark (plants the Chapter 5 twist). MARKER CUES: {m:version} the second sheet slides in; {m:think} the 0.5 s Gondwana watermark flicker.

segments.text: But the shapes are just the {m:first}first clue. The next one is on the {m:far}far side of the planet.
segments.visual: At {m:first}: the seven drip arrows flash once on the cold-open globe while the camera pushes in. At {m:far}: hard cut to the cutawayEarth stage with the North Pole on top; drillDir draws the cyan line from the pole through the core and out the South Pole in 1.4 s while the camera dollies from [6,3.5,6] to [4.5,2.6,4.5] (target [0,0.3,0], fov 32).
segments.music: Riser into Chapter 2; switch to the pulsing synth + strings data bed.

segments.text: Start at the top of the world. The {m:np}North Pole isn't land, it's ocean. Which makes Santa's workshop, technically, a {m:boat}houseboat. Stand on the ice there, and the sea floor is about {m:depth}two and a half miles beneath your boots.
segments.visual: Chapter card as a 2 s overlay on moving footage. Camera flies to {lat:85, lon:0, alt:1.4, tilt:35}: the dark bathymetric Arctic basin ringed by land (the texture has no sea ice). At {m:np}: pulsing white marker + pill. At {m:boat}: EXPLORER GAG 3 (3D diorama stage): the Explorer on a white floe slab bobbing on a dark water plane beside a red-and-white striped pole (simple cylinder); optional low-poly cabin with chimney smoke on the next floe. At {m:depth}: cut to a 2D PROFILE PANEL (slice Greenland -> pole -> Siberia): thin white ice line, navy water, sea floor 2.5 mi down; a depth ruler drops from the ice to the floor; the Explorer (same stage, transparent background, composited on the ice line) looks down and recoils (HitRecieve_2).
segments.humor: Santa's workshop is technically a houseboat. EXPLORER GAG 3: vertigo over two and a half miles of water (HitRecieve_2).

segments.text: Now go to the {m:bottom}bottom. At the {m:sp}South Pole, you're standing almost {m:up}two miles up, on a {m:sheet}sheet of ice more than a mile and a half {m:thick}thick.
segments.visual: At {m:bottom}: the profile panel whips down to a South Pole profile on the same axis scale: dashed sea-level line, rock below, white ice sheet above. At {m:sp}: marker SOUTH POLE. At {m:up}: the ice column rises under the Explorer like an elevator to almost 2 miles (upward ruler); on 'a mile and a half thick' a bracket draws along the ice. He stands on top (Idle_Neutral), beard flapping. Schematic, not to scale (the Explorer is a gag, not a scale reference). MARKER CUES: {m:sheet} the white ice sheet is outlined; {m:thick} the bracket draws along the ice.

segments.text: The two ends of the planet are {m:neg}photographic negatives. Ocean on top. A continent at the bottom.
segments.visual: Mode change: two 2D POLAR DISCS (520 px, azimuthal equal-area from ne_50m_land; Antarctica includes ice shelves), slowly counter-rotating. Left: Arctic, navy ocean centre with a cream ring of land. Right: Antarctica, cream land centre with a navy ring of ocean. At {m:neg}: the Arctic disc inverts via a 'difference' composite against white (cream and navy swap over 0.4 s) and now rhymes with the Antarctic disc.
onscreen: OCEAN ON TOP. LAND AT BOTTOM.

segments.text: And they're almost the same size. {m:drag}Drag the Arctic Ocean down onto Antarctica, and the sizes nearly {m:match}match.
segments.visual: Globe. At {m:drag}: www/geo/arctic_ocean.geojson rings (cyan) are dragged with `moves` (true size) along the 0 deg meridian over 2.5 s; the camera tracks the shape's centroid at alt 2.6 from lat 70 to lat -70. At {m:match}: it settles over Antarctica (outlined orange); the two areas almost coincide.

segments.text: But here's the part that doesn't make sense. They don't just match. They {m:line}line up. Most of {m:ant}Antarctica sits directly opposite the Arctic Ocean, on the exact {m:other}other side of the Earth.
segments.visual: Music cuts 0.5 s before {m:line}. At {m:line}: cutawayEarth stage (North Pole on top), drillDir shoots from the pole through the core into Antarctica in 1.2 s. At {m:ant}: cut to the globe looking straight down on the Arctic {lat:90, alt:2.4}: arctic_ocean.geojson outlined cyan; Antarctica's outline mirrored to its antipode (lat -> -lat, lon -> lon+180) draws on in orange. At {m:other}: the overlap of mirrored Antarctica and the Arctic Ocean fills yellow. FIRST JAW-DROP (~3:00).
onscreen: MOST OF ANTARCTICA: OPPOSITE THE ARCTIC OCEAN
segments.music: Cut the bed 0.5 s before 'line up'.

segments.text: And it's not just the {m:poles}poles. Almost everywhere you look, land has {m:avoid}ocean on its far side, not more land. Which {m:brings}brings us to a classic American playground {m:myth}myth.
segments.visual: Pull back to the whole globe. At {m:avoid}: a 1.0 s glimpse of tex/data/antipodes.png fading on and off (cyan flipped land, small yellow overlaps). At {m:myth}: kinetic headline. MARKER CUES: {m:poles} pull back to the whole globe; {m:brings} the headline words start rising, landing on {m:myth}.

segments.text: If you dig straight down, you'll reach {m:china}China. Let's {m:test}test it. Start in {m:kansas}Kansas, right at the center of the lower forty-eight, and {m:dig}dig. Ignore everything on the way down that would kill you, and keep {m:going}going.
segments.visual: At {m:china}: globe centred on China (35N 105E, alt 2.6), China fills orange. At {m:test}: whip west to the US (39N 98W); China is on the far side and cannot share the frame. At {m:kansas}: marker drops on the 1918 geographic centre of the lower 48 (39.83N 98.58W, near Lebanon, Kansas) + pill. At {m:dig}: EXPLORER GAG 4a (tiny planet, Kansas rotated to the top): he touches the ground (Interact) and a glowing beam fires straight down from his hand; moveAlong lowers him 0.6 units into the planet over 1.2 s until he vanishes (2D dirt puffs). Then cut to cutawayEarth with Kansas on top: drillDir runs from Kansas through the core over ~3 s with a tiny Explorer icon riding the drill head; no depth numbers. At {m:going}: the drill nears the far side.
segments.humor: 'Ignore everything on the way down that would kill you.' EXPLORER GAG 4a: digs from Kansas (Interact) and sinks out of sight.

segments.text: You come out in the {m:indian}southern Indian Ocean. The {m:nearest}nearest land is a tiny French {m:island}island, more than two hundred miles {m:away}away.
segments.visual: The drill exits at the bottom of the cutaway. At {m:indian}: tiny planet rotated so 39.83S 81.42E (Kansas's antipode) is on top, all blue; the Explorer shoots up out of the water (moveAlong y -0.6 -> +0.4), Roll, then Idle chest-deep inside a 2D ripple ring, the whole model bobbing on the swell (treading water). At {m:nearest}: cut to the photoreal globe over the antipode {alt:0.35, tilt:40}: yellow pulsing marker, a dashed great-circle line draws to Ile Saint-Paul (38.72S 77.53E), shown as a tiny white dot with no label. MARKER CUES: {m:island} the tiny white dot pops; {m:away} the pill swaps to the distance.
segments.humor: EXPLORER GAG 4b: pops out into empty ocean and treads water (Roll, Idle).

segments.text: Not {m:notchina}China. Not even the right {m:hemi}hemisphere. In fact, there isn't a single spot in the {m:us}United States that sits opposite {m:china2}China.
segments.visual: Equal Earth flat map (place and antipode both on screen): all 50 states mirrored in cyan (lower 48 in the Indian Ocean, Hawaii on Botswana, a sliver of Alaska on Antarctica), China in orange. At {m:china2}: they touch nowhere; JUICE CHECK: FALSE stamp. MARKER CUES: {m:notchina} cut to the flat map, China orange; {m:hemi} the equator line flashes between the Kansas antipode (south) and China (north); {m:us} the mirrored cyan states draw on.

segments.text: Even if you {m:start}started in China, three times out of {m:four}four you'd surface in the ocean. The people who can actually {m:dig2}dig to China? {m:arg}Argentinians.
segments.visual: Flat map. At {m:start}: China's antipodal outline (cyan) draws on over the South Pacific and South Atlantic off Chile and Argentina. At {m:four}: the part over water fills cyan; about a quarter (over Argentina and Chile) fills yellow. At {m:arg}: Argentina fills orange and its own antipodal outline lands right on China (overlap yellow). A Kenney mini (mini_male_a, separate stage, transparent background, ~110 px) pops up out of a little hole in China (jump) and plays emote-yes. Then a 1 s cutaway: the Explorer still bobbing alone in the Indian Ocean (Idle). MARKER CUES: {m:dig2} a tiny shovel icon taps Argentina.
segments.humor: Punchline 'Argentinians.' Kenney mini pops out in China; the Explorer is still stranded at sea.

segments.text: Now flip {m:flipall}every continent to the far side of the planet and {m:lay}lay it over the {m:orig}original. Only about {m:eighth}one-eighth of the land has land on the other side.
segments.visual: Equal Earth flat map (area-true, so the polar pair is not inflated). At {m:flipall}: the reprojected antipodes.png cyan layer wipes in left to right over grey real land. At {m:orig}: the yellow overlaps pulse one at a time: South America with East Asia, Antarctica with the Arctic lands, New Zealand with Spain (1.5x punch-in). At {m:eighth}: hero counter. MARKER CUES: {m:lay} the cyan wipe completes.

segments.text: That's less than half of what you'd expect if the continents had been {m:random}sprinkled at random.
segments.visual: Mode change: DATA CARD on navy with two 10x10 waffle grids of land squares, left IF RANDOM, right REAL EARTH. At {m:random}: squares light yellow (land with land opposite) in a fast random order; the left stops at 29 squares, the right at 13; a white bracket shows the right is under half. No numbers printed (hero-number rule); the grids carry the ratio.

segments.text: So try a {m:puzzle}puzzle. Slice the Earth into {m:half}two halves, any way you like, and {m:cram}cram as much land as you can into one of them.
segments.visual: Back to the globe. At {m:half}: a translucent hemisphere cap (hemisphereCanvas regenerated each frame at 1024x512, source-in against the land mask: land inside the cap glows orange, ocean inside stays cyan) sweeps along a scripted search path that ends at 40N 2E. MARKER CUES: {m:puzzle} a small puzzle-piece icon pops; {m:cram} the cap's search speeds up.

segments.text: The winner is centered on {m:europe}western Europe. It scoops up most of the world's land. And it's still {m:still}more than half water.
segments.visual: The cap settles centred between Brittany and the Spanish coast (40N 2E) at {m:europe}; land inside glows. Music cuts 0.5 s before {m:still}; at {m:still} the ocean inside the cap floods cyan.

segments.text: There is no way to {m:cut}cut this planet in half and get a half that's {m:mostly}mostly land.
segments.visual: Mode change: a 2x3 grid of pre-rendered globe stills (still.cjs), each with a hemisphere cap centred on Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica and Australia (ocean inside the cap cyan, land orange). A red X stamp icon (no words) slams onto each tile, 1.0 s apart; tiles drift slightly. MARKER CUES: {m:cut} the 2x3 grid slides in; the X stamps then land 1.0 s apart. MARKER CUES: {m:mostly} the last X lands and the headline pill appears.

segments.text: Now flip the globe {m:flip}over. The other half is {m:p89}eighty-nine percent water, centered in the empty Pacific near New Zealand.
segments.visual: Globe centred (-40,-178). It whips 180 deg at {m:flip}; the opposite cap goes deep cyan. At {m:p89}: hero counter climbs to 89%; New Zealand is a small orange sliver near the cap's centre.

segments.text: The Pacific {m:alone}alone could swallow {m:drop}every continent on Earth, with room to spare. Yes, even {m:asia}Asia.
segments.visual: Globe on the Pacific {lat:-5, lon:-160, alt:2.6}. At {m:alone}: the Pacific (NE 10m marine polygons incl. marginal seas) outlined cyan. From {m:drop}: continents lift off as orange shapes (moves, 0.5 s apart) and 'melt' into an AREA-TRUE orange pour spreading out from the basin centre (offline raster: Pacific cells ordered by distance from the centre, filled until the filled area equals the land dropped so far; rigid true-size packing would overlap and is NOT used). EXPLORER GAG 5: Australia arrives carrying the still-soaked Explorer (stage render composited at the shape's projected centroid, ~140 px, Idle_Neutral). Asia drops LAST at {m:asia} with the heaviest thunk; its splash rocks him (HitRecieve_2). The pour stops leaving a blue rim; pull out wide; he waves from the leftover blue (Wave).
segments.humor: Tag 'Yes, even Asia.' EXPLORER GAG 5: hitches a ride on Australia, gets rocked by Asia's splash, waves from the leftover room (Idle_Neutral, HitRecieve_2, Wave).

segments.text: {m:ocean}Ocean on top, {m:landb}land at the bottom, {m:avoidl}land avoiding land. This planet is strangely {m:lop}lopsided. And the drip might be just the part you can {m:see}see.
segments.visual: Callback montage, ~1 s each: polar discs, antipode flat map, water-half cap. At {m:lop}: return to the s001 tilted drip globe (core question restated, ~36%). MARKER CUES: {m:ocean} polar discs; {m:landb} Antarctic disc; {m:avoidl} antipode flat map; {m:see} the drip arcs redraw on the s001 globe.
onscreen: WHY DO THE CONTINENTS POINT SOUTH?

segments.text: And back in {m:g1875}eighteen seventy-five, one man thought he'd found a single {m:shape}shape that explained all of it. And it wasn't a {m:ball}ball.
segments.visual: Sepia wipe. At {m:g1875}: tetraEarth at k=0 with edge opacity 0.9; the edges sit at 1.55R, so the four yellow corners poke out through the surface (a pyramid hidden inside the planet). At {m:ball}: the four corners flare. Keep it rotating under the subscribe ask so the loop stays open on screen. MARKER CUES: {m:shape} the hidden yellow edges start glowing.
segments.music: Riser; switch to curious felt piano + pizzicato.

segments.text: Before we meet him: every Myth Juice video takes {m:taught}one thing you were taught about the world and {m:checks}checks it against the real planet. Want the next one? {m:sub}Subscribe.
segments.visual: Picture keeps moving: slow orbit of the rotating tetra-in-globe. At {m:taught}: the brand JUICE CHECK stamp spins in at upper left. At {m:checks}: it lands with a '?' on the hidden pyramid (the next verdict is pending). At {m:sub}: an animated subscribe button glows in the lower third, above the bottom 12%. No freeze. FIRST SUBSCRIBE ASK (~37%), right after the China / 89% / Pacific payoffs, inside the open 1875 loop.

segments.text: His name was William Lowthian Green. He wasn't a professor. He was the {m:hawaii}foreign minister of the Kingdom of Hawaii.
segments.visual: Chapter card (2 s overlay). Ken Burns (4x) on Green's 1875 title page (archive.org vestigesmolteng00greegoog leaf n5 at w1600; crop out the Bodleian stamp and handwritten shelfmark). At {m:hawaii}: the line 'MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS TO THE KING OF THE SANDWICH ISLANDS' gets an orange highlight; quick cut to a pulsing marker on Hawaii.
segments.humor: Reveal: the theorist was Hawaii's foreign minister.

segments.text: And he'd been {m:obsessed}obsessed with those pointy southern tips for years. He even demonstrated them with a {m:card}bent card dipped in {m:water}water.
segments.visual: Small 3D diorama: two 1.2x0.8 white planes hinged at 165 deg (a shallow roof), tilted 8 deg nose-down; at {m:card} it lowers into a cyan water plane (0.6 opacity); the dry part reads as a triangle aimed at the dipped end, with a white line along the waterline. Cross-dissolve to Green's Figure 1 (assets/pd/green_n18.jpg; NOT green_fig1.jpg, which is a blank page): the south-pointing three-lobed 'normal form'. MARKER CUES (reordered): {m:obsessed} Ken Burns on Green's Figure 1 (assets/pd/green_n18.jpg) first; {m:card} the card diorama; {m:water} the card touches the water and the dry triangle appears.

segments.text: Remember those {m:pyr2}'pyramidal' tips? Green thought the whole planet was heading that way: {m:cool}cooling, shrinking, and slowly collapsing toward a {m:tet}tetrahedron. A four-cornered {m:pyr4}pyramid.
segments.visual: At {m:pyr2}: 1 s callback flash of Humboldt's triangle outlines on the s020 globe. Then the tetraEarth stage (radius 2.2) with the Explorer standing on top (the North Pole = centre of the future top face). At {m:tet}: k ramps 0 -> 1 over 3 s while the whole group tilts 25 deg toward camera so the top face slopes; EXPLORER GAG 6a: he Rolls (moveAlong) from the face centre down to the near upper corner (19.47N, -75, the Americas vertex). At {m:pyr4}: he stops perched on that corner (Idle_Neutral) and stays there through s053; the yellow edges flare. MARKER CUES: {m:cool} inward 'cooling' arrows ring the planet as the Explorer stands on top.
segments.humor: EXPLORER GAG 6a: the ground tilts under him as the planet turns into a pyramid; he rolls down to a corner and perches (Roll, Idle_Neutral).
sfx: slide whistle down (generate CC0; fallback whoosh_soft -14)

segments.text: It sounds ridiculous. But watch what it {m:pred}explained. Most land in the north: {m:c1}check. Three continents ending in points aimed south: {m:c2}check.
segments.visual: Checklist, one line at a time (each replaces the previous; never more than two text elements). Each tick gets its own lookFrom on the tetra (Explorer still perched): {m:c1} side view, north up, three upper corners; {m:c2} low side view along an edge running down to the south vertex. MARKER CUES: {m:pred} the checklist frame slides in beside the tetra.

segments.text: An ocean on top of the world: {m:c3}check. A continent at the bottom: {m:c4}check. Land sitting opposite water: {m:c5}check. One shape, every clue.
segments.visual: {m:c3}: view from straight above at the flat top face (Arctic); {m:c4}: view from straight below at the south vertex (Antarctica); {m:c5}: a vertex with the opposite face behind it. Then a '5 / 5' stamp.

segments.text: And it went {m:main}mainstream. By eighteen ninety-nine, a leading {m:geol}geologist was telling Britain's top geographers that a shrinking Earth had to {m:squeeze}squeeze toward a {m:geo}tetrahedron.
segments.visual: At {m:main}: Ken Burns across the fetched March 1899 journal leaf with the Fig. 5 tetrahedron diagrams (archive.org sim_geographical-journal_1899-03_13_3; frame out the masthead, no citation look). At {m:geo}: orange underline under 'tending to become tetrahedral', then cut to the rotating tetraEarth with a '1899' pill and the Explorer still clinging to his corner. Fallback if the leaf is unusable: sepia-graded tetraEarth + the pill (do NOT substitute Green's 1875 figure). MARKER CUES: {m:geol} the 1899 journal leaf Ken Burns starts; {m:squeeze} the Ken Burns pushes into the Fig. 5 tetrahedron.

segments.text: He even pointed out that most of North America sits opposite the {m:io}Indian Ocean. The same ocean you just dug into.
segments.visual: Globe over the Indian Ocean: North America mirrored to its antipode in cyan; the lower 48 and Mexico land in the Indian Ocean, while Greenland and Arctic Canada land on Antarctica (keep that visible: it is why the line says 'most'). At {m:io}: the same yellow pulsing marker at 39.83S 81.42E (Kansas's antipode) reappears inside the cyan outline with the same sonar ping.
onscreen: MOST OF NORTH AMERICA: OPPOSITE INDIAN OCEAN
segments.humor: Callback to the dig gag.

segments.text: By nineteen eighteen, a children's {m:mag}magazine was telling kids that one day, the Earth would turn into a {m:pyramid}pyramid. Sleep {m:tight}tight, kids.
segments.visual: Recreated sepia children's-page card (our own typography, no real masthead). Kenney mini characters sit cross-legged (sit) facing a chalkboard where a globe morphs into a pyramid at {m:pyramid}. At {m:tight}: one mini turns to camera and plays emote-no. MARKER CUES: {m:mag} the recreated children's-page card and the seated minis appear.
segments.humor: Deadpan 'Sleep tight, kids.' (Kenney mini emote-no).

segments.text: So, hang on. If it explained all that, {m:how}how do we know it's wrong?
segments.visual: The tetrahedron freezes mid-turn (Explorer perched; keep a 1 deg/s drift so the frame is not static); music drops out at {m:how}; a single '?' draws itself on one face.
segments.music: Silence 0.9 s.

segments.text: Because the whole idea needed a cooling, shrinking Earth. And critics could {m:measure}measure the planet: a ball, slightly squashed at the poles. Not a {m:notp}pyramid. And by then, scientists had discovered {m:rad}radioactivity, quietly heating Earth from the inside.
segments.visual: Inward 'shrinking' arrows (2D) appear around the tetra. At {m:measure}: a measuring-tape graphic wraps the planet and a white oblate ellipse outline (labelled EXAGGERATED) overlays it. At {m:notp}: a red X on the tetra outline. At {m:rad}: glowing orange specks (2D sprites over the model) speckle the interior with a soft heat glow.

segments.text: Over the next few decades, the shrinking engine {m:stall}stalled. The pyramid vanished from geology. Green's checklist was {m:real}real. He'd just pinned the clues on the wrong {m:suspect}suspect.
segments.visual: At {m:stall}: the inward arrows stall and FADE (never reverse; no outward arrows: Earth is not expanding). EXPLORER GAG 6b: the tetra puffs back into a round sphere (k 1 -> 0, E.outBack); his corner disappears from under him (HitRecieve_2) and he ends standing on the round globe, looking around for his corner (Idle_Neutral). ~3 s. At {m:real}: Green's globe engravings (assets/pd/green_globes.jpg, Figs 9-10) drift by in sepia; five icon-only clue cards appear on a dark board (ocean cap, Antarctica, south-pointing triangle, north-heavy globe, antipode double-arrow). At {m:suspect}: red strings link all five to a tetrahedron icon, which gets a red X.
segments.humor: EXPLORER GAG 6b: the pyramid pops back into a ball and his corner vanishes from under him (HitRecieve_2, Idle_Neutral). Detective framing: 'wrong suspect'.

segments.text: The real suspect had been hiding in plain sight on every world {m:maps}map. It took one stubborn man to {m:say}say it out loud. And his story ends on one of the {m:drips}drips.
segments.visual: At {m:maps}: Ken Burns across Ortelius's 1570 Typus Orbis Terrarum (PD; fetch from Commons), pushing in on the Atlantic; orange glowPaths trace the facing coasts of South America and Africa. At {m:say}: cross-dissolve to the photoreal globe {lat:-10, lon:-15, alt:2.4}, same two coasts glowing; the continents twitch apart 0.3 deg (moves, 0.2 s). At {m:drips}: 1 s Greenland tip-pop on the s003 flat map with the cold-open thump, then dip to white.
segments.music: Riser into Chapter 4.

segments.text: Around nineteen ten, a young German weather scientist named Alfred Wegener {m:wrote}wrote to his future wife. Doesn't South America {m:fit}fit against Africa, he asked, as if they had once been {m:joined}joined?
segments.visual: Chapter card (2 s overlay). Ken Burns on the Wegener portrait (assets/pd/wegener_portrait.jpg, c.1924-30, PD in US). At {m:wrote}: the Ken Burns lands on the eyes and an envelope icon slides in. At {m:fit}: the Atlantic coasts of both continents glow white on the globe. At {m:joined}: South America slides east (moves) and nestles against Africa.
onscreen: WHY DID GEOLOGISTS LAUGH AT WEGENER?
segments.music: Chapter 4: hopeful strings that later turn cold.

segments.text: 'This is an idea I'll have to {m:pursue}pursue.'
segments.visual: Handwritten-style letter card (Playfair Display 700 italic) with the line; the fitted continents glow behind it. MARKER CUES: {m:pursue} the handwritten line finishes writing on.

segments.text: In nineteen twelve, he stood up before a {m:meeting}meeting of geologists and told them the {m:move}continents move. Then a world {m:war}war buried his {m:book}book.
segments.visual: At {m:move}: a 3 s simplified paleo scrub on the globe from 200 Ma to today (paleo/coast_TTT.json; years chip 'MILLION YEARS AGO · SIMPLIFIED'): real reconstructed motion, not invented arrows. (The on-disk wegener_1924_fig4.jpg is a hypsometric curve, not a reconstruction map: do not use it here.) At {m:war}: dark smoke rolls across the frame and a simple book silhouette stamped 1915 sinks under it. MARKER CUES: {m:meeting} a 1912 pill over the portrait; {m:book} the 1915 book silhouette sinks under the smoke.

segments.text: Once the world read it, the reaction was {m:brutal}brutal. One society president called it {m:rot}'utter, damned rot.' In Germany, he never landed a full {m:prof}professorship. It took a university in {m:austria}Austria to give him one.
segments.visual: EXPLORER GAG 7: at {m:rot} a quote card slams into frame; the Explorer, standing beside a small drifting globe, recoils as if hit by the words (HitRecieve). At {m:prof}: a row of simple university-door icons slam shut one by one. At {m:austria}: one door at the far end opens onto warm light; a marker pops on Graz. MARKER CUES: {m:brutal} five generic book silhouettes (the 1922 translations) fan out around the Explorer.
segments.humor: EXPLORER GAG 7: knocked back by an insult (HitRecieve).

segments.text: And critics had one killer question: what could possibly {m:push}push a continent? Wegener guessed Earth's {m:spin}spin, and tides. Both were far too {m:weak}weak.
segments.visual: At {m:push}: a big '?' over the continents. At {m:spin}: curved white spin arrows on the globe and a tidal-bulge graphic pushing on a continent. At {m:weak}: a 2D needle gauge labelled FORCE twitches and sags to near zero.
onscreen: SPIN AND TIDES: FAR TOO WEAK

segments.text: He admitted it himself. 'The Newton of drift theory has not yet {m:appeared}appeared.'
segments.visual: Wegener portrait again, slow push toward the eyes; the quote types on. MARKER CUES: {m:appeared} the quote finishes typing.
onscreen: "THE NEWTON OF DRIFT... NOT YET APPEARED"

segments.text: In nineteen thirty, Wegener was deep on the ice of {m:grl}Greenland. One of the drip's own tips.
segments.visual: At {m:grl}: Greenland pops orange on the globe with the same tip-pop thump as the cold open; then a low flyover across the white Greenland ice sheet toward its centre (patch tex/patch/greenland.jpg, relief 1.0, tilt 50, ~10 s).
segments.music: Sparse cold drone and wind.

segments.text: On his {m:fifty}fiftieth birthday, he left a {m:camp}camp in the middle of the ice sheet with a Greenlander named Rasmus {m:villumsen}Villumsen.
segments.visual: Slow Ken Burns on the last photo of Wegener and Villumsen (assets/pd/wegener_last_026.jpg = Commons 'Wegener Expedition-1930 026.jpg', tagged PD-Mark; VERIFY the licence on the live Commons page / with AWI before use; fallback: a verified-PD expedition image or a recreated still of two figures and a sled on the ice). Hold at {m:fifty}. MARKER CUES: {m:camp} the Ken Burns drifts across the photo; {m:villumsen} it settles on the second figure.

segments.text: Neither of them made it {m:back}back.
segments.visual: The photo slowly fades to pure white (exposure ramp over 3 s). No Explorer anywhere in s063-s068. MARKER CUES: {m:back} the fade to white begins.
segments.music: Music drops to silence; wind only.

segments.text: They found Wegener's body the next {m:may}May, carefully buried in the snow. Villumsen was never {m:found}found.
segments.visual: Flyover resumes over empty ice; light snowfall; no location marker. MARKER CUES: {m:may} the 'FOUND: MAY 1931' pill; {m:found} the snowfall thickens and the pill fades.

segments.text: Wegener never saw his idea proven. The proof was hiding on the {m:floor}ocean floor: stripes of magnetized rock, {m:mirror}mirrored on both sides of the mid-ocean ridges, like a {m:tape}tape recording of new seafloor being made.
segments.visual: Cut from white ice to the dark ocean floor. At {m:floor}: magnetic 'zebra' stripes (recreated schematic) appear. At {m:mirror}: they mirror across a glowing mid-ocean ridge. At {m:tape}: new stripes emerge at the centre and slide outward symmetrically like tape leaving a recorder.
segments.music: Slow warm swell returns.

segments.text: It came out {m:y33}thirty-three years after he died.
segments.visual: Year counter rolls 1930 -> 1963 at {m:y33}; the stripes lock into place.
segments.music: Warm music comes back up before 'Today' so the next joke reads as a deliberate release.

segments.text: Today, satellites clock the continents moving at about the speed your {m:nail}fingernails grow. Or your {m:toe}toenails, depending on which government agency you ask.
segments.visual: Globe on the Atlantic: white GPS-style velocity arrows appear on the plates. At {m:nail}: a split diagram slides in from the right (mode change): a vector fingertip whose nail edge creeps forward. At {m:toe}: boxing fight-card split: a vector foot icon slides in opposite with 'VS' between them; the two icons tilt toward each other as if arguing. No agency names or labels.
segments.humor: Fingernails vs toenails: the agencies disagree (fight card).

segments.text: So Wegener was {m:right}right. But that still doesn't explain the {m:drip}drip. Why would so many of them end up {m:point}pointing the same way?
segments.visual: Pull back to the tilted drip globe; the southern tips glow; at {m:point} a big '?' hangs over Antarctica's ring (core question restated, ~62%). MARKER CUES: {m:right} JUICE CHECK: TRUE stamp over Wegener's portrait (brand verdict); {m:drip} cut to the tilted drip globe.

segments.text: Run the clock {m:rewind}backwards, and the big drips all start pointing at the same {m:place}place.
segments.visual: Mode change: black scrub card; a time-scrub bar slides in (above the bottom 12%); at {m:rewind} its counter starts rolling backwards. At {m:place}: the drip arrows on the three big tips swing toward one point off-frame below.
segments.music: Building swell begins.

segments.text: Back into the age of dinosaurs. Watch the southern continents slide home: {m:r_sam}South America, {m:r_afr}Africa, {m:r_ind}India, {m:r_aus}Australia.
segments.visual: Chapter card (2 s overlay). Paleo globe (PaleoOverlay; look {flatBase:1, ovAlpha:1, ovMul:1, nightAmt:0, relief:0}) from a south-polar camera {lat:-60, lon:20, alt:2.8} so Gondwana assembles centre-frame; T scrubs 0 -> 180 Ma across the segment (E.inOut). Polygon indices are mapped to continents once from coast_000.json centroids; on each name marker that continent's polygons fill orange. MARKER CUES: {m:r_sam}, {m:r_afr}, {m:r_ind}, {m:r_aus} each continent's polygons fill orange on its name.
segments.music: Building swell continues.

segments.text: They lock together into one supercontinent: {m:gond}Gondwana. And at its heart sits {m:ant}Antarctica. Geologists call it the keypiece.
segments.visual: Pieces lock with a clunk at {m:gond}; at {m:ant} Antarctica pulses with a yellow ring at the centre of the assembled Gondwana.

segments.text: {m:remember}Remember Bacon's open question? Is there even a southern continent? The drips were {m:point}pointing at it {m:whole}the whole time.
segments.visual: At {m:remember}: cut for 2.5 s to Bacon's portrait (sepia, Ken Burns toward the eyes) with the question pill (breaks the long paleo run). At {m:point}: back to the assembled Gondwana paleo globe. At {m:whole}: white drip arrows from the 180 Ma positions of cape_horn, cape_agulhas and kanyakumari (paleo/tracks.json) converge on the yellow ring at the south_pole track point.
segments.music: Music cut 0.5 s before 'the whole time', then swell.

segments.text: Now let the clock run {m:fwd}forward. Cracks open, and new ocean starts seeping in between {m:afant}Africa and Antarctica.
segments.visual: At {m:fwd}: the counter starts running forward from 180 Ma. At {m:afant}: a thin blue line of new ocean cracks open between Africa and Antarctica.

segments.text: Then the {m:zip}South Atlantic unzips from the bottom up, {m:split}splitting Africa from South America. The south tears open {m:firstt}first. The last {m:seam}seam, near the equator, hangs on for millions of years {m:snap2}more.
segments.visual: At {m:zip}: the South Atlantic opens like a zipper from its south end northward, a zipper-pull icon tracking the opening. The equatorial link holds, then snaps at {m:snap2}. MARKER CUES: {m:split} Africa and South America glow on either side of the opening; {m:firstt} the southern gap widens; {m:seam} the equatorial link glows yellow before it snaps.

segments.text: And then everyone moves {m:leave}out. Except {m:stay}Antarctica. It barely budges. It keeps the {m:house}house.
segments.visual: T runs 140 -> 60 Ma: Africa, South America, India and Australia drift north out of frame while Antarctica stays centred. EXPLORER GAG 8: the Explorer stage (transparent background) is composited over the paleo globe at the projected south_pole track point (~150 px). At {m:leave}: he waves goodbye (Wave) to the departing continents. At {m:stay}: Antarctica's yellow ring pulses under him. At {m:house}: a tiny porch light flicks on behind him.
segments.humor: Breakup metaphor: everyone moves out, Antarctica keeps the house. EXPLORER GAG 8: left behind, waving everyone off (Wave).

segments.text: India {m:sprint}sprints: up to about eight inches a year, several times faster than {m:afaus}Africa or Australia. For a continent, that's reckless {m:driving}driving. Then it {m:slam}slams into Asia.
segments.visual: At {m:sprint}: India streaks north with a glowing speed trail; its speed tag gets cartoon motion lines. At {m:slam}: it crashes into Asia with a shock ring. MARKER CUES: {m:afaus} Africa and Australia crawl beside India with short trails; {m:driving} cartoon motion lines on India's speed tag.
onscreen: INDIA: UP TO ~8 INCHES A YEAR
segments.humor: 'For a continent, that's reckless driving.'

segments.text: Here's the best {m:best}explanation geologists have. Put the pieces back {m:together}together, and their pointy ends are the ones that sat right up against {m:ant2}Antarctica.
segments.visual: Counter jumps back to 180 Ma. At {m:ant2}: the southern tips of South America, Africa and India pulse orange exactly where they touch Antarctica's ring. MARKER CUES: {m:best} counter jumps back to 180 Ma; {m:together} the pieces re-lock around Antarctica.

segments.text: As they drifted {m:apart}apart, they roughly kept their orientation. So those points still {m:aim}aim back to where they tore away.
segments.visual: Counter runs to TODAY; camera pulls back to the present-day tilted globe (the s001 angle). At {m:apart}: dotted yellow lines draw the real paths from paleo/tracks.json (cape_horn, cape_agulhas, kanyakumari, 0 -> 180 Ma) on today's globe. At {m:aim}: they converge near Antarctica's ring.
segments.music: Music cut 0.5 s before the next line.

segments.text: The big drips aren't drips at all. They're {m:scar}scars.
segments.visual: At {m:scar}: the dotted trails turn into glowing seam lines, like healed scars across the oceans.
segments.music: Swell lands on 'scars'.

segments.text: Back to that second drip joke. The geologist who wrote it was John {m:holden}Holden.
segments.visual: The 1976 typewriter sheet from Chapter 1 returns; at {m:holden} its blurred byline un-blurs to JOHN C. HOLDEN.
segments.music: Playful pizzicato returns.

segments.text: Writing for a science humor journal, he declared that every continent is a {m:tear}teardrop, with the pointed end showing the direction it came from.
segments.visual: At {m:tear}: teardrop silhouettes (each sized to its continent's area, centred on its centroid, point aimed south) fade in over the dimmed continents with a white outline draw-on (0.6 s). Our own redraw, not the copyrighted figure.

segments.text: Drips always flow {m:down}down, he reasoned, so our maps must be {m:upside}upside down. He was {m:joking}joking. But one of the most famous {m:photo}photos of Earth ever taken really was shot with {m:bm}Antarctica on top. It was published {m:flip}flipped.

At {m:bm}: assets/pd/bluemarble_original.jpg (Apollo 17, south-up, PD) fills the frame. At {m:flip}: it rotates 180 deg and dissolves into assets/pd/bluemarble_northup.jpg. MARKER CUES: {m:down} a single teardrop falls down the frame; {m:joking} a 'JOKE' tag wobbles onto the flipped globe; {m:photo} cut to a photo frame drawing on, filled at {m:bm}.

segments.text: So by Holden's logic, it was right the first {m:first}time.

segments.text: And one day, he wrote, the continents would {m:splash}splash back together into a supercontinent called {m:pangooy}'Pangooy.' On a {m:tue}Tuesday, at nine in the morning. He did not say which {m:tz}time zone.

segments.text: {m:twist}Here's the twist. Six years {m:earlier}earlier, the very same John Holden had helped map, for {m:real}real, how Pangaea broke {m:apart2}apart.

Split screen: left, our own serious breakup still (paleo coast_200 with motion trails to today, labelled '1970: THE REAL MAP (SIMPLIFIED)'); right, the joke teardrop map (our redraw). At {m:apart2}: a yellow line links the two under the same name. MARKER CUES: {m:earlier} the left panel (real map) slides in; {m:real} the right panel (joke) slides in.

segments.text: And the joke wasn't {m:notdone}done. Geologists have since found {m:realdrip}real drips. Under {m:nev}Nevada, a cold blob of rock appears to be sinking into the Earth, like {m:honey}honey off a spoon. One of the scientists who found it admitted he'd been {m:anti}'anti-drip' since his early days.

segments.text: Now, the honest {m:honest}part, because we're not going to fake you a tidy answer. Not everything {m:drips}drips.

segments.text: And Africa's real southern tip isn't the Cape of Good {m:gh}Hope. It's Cape {m:agul}Agulhas, and the best-known story says the name means {m:needles}'needles,' because sailors' {m:compass}compass needles there pointed true north. So Africa's southern tip is named after pointing {m:north2}north.

MARKER CUES: {m:likely} the JUICE CHECK stamp lands; {m:single} the small-drip icons flicker.

segments.text: Give it a couple hundred million {m:years}years, and geologists think a new supercontinent will {m:form}form. They just can't {m:agree}agree on what it looks like. Here are the four main {m:models}models.
